question: What happens to the bread and wine in the Eucharist, and how is Christ present?

positions.name: Memorial

defined.source: Huldrych Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles, Article 18 (1523)
defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: The Lord's Supper is a symbolic act of obedience whereby members of the church, through partaking of the bread and the fruit of the vine, memorialize the death of the Redeemer and anticipate His second coming.

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: a memorial of his suffering and death

positions.statement: The bread and wine are symbols that call Christ's death to mind; Christ's body and blood are neither present in them nor received through them.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread and wine only represent or remind of Christ's body and blood, and that nothing more than this remembrance is given in the rite.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says believers truly receive Christ's body and blood in the Supper, in any manner.
positions.first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523); Baptist Faith and Message (1925, revised 2000)
positions.notes: Not all Baptists hold it: the 1689 Baptist Confession teaches spiritual presence. Pentecostal placement rests on the Assemblies of God text; other Pentecostal bodies are silent. 'Pentecostal' here means the classical Pentecostal denominations (Assemblies of God, Church of God, IPHC); charismatics inside other churches hold their own church's position.

positions.name: Spiritual presence

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 29.7 (1646)
defined.quote: the body and blood of Christ being then, not corporally or carnally, in, with, or under the bread and wine; yet, as really, but spiritually, present to the faith of believers in that ordinance

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXVIII (1571)
defined.quote: The Body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten, in the Supper, only after an heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the Body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is Faith.

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 30.7 (1689)
defined.quote: spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified, and all the benefits of his death

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in the Supper, only after a heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is faith.

defined.source: Confession of Faith of the Evangelical United Brethren Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: partake of the body and blood of Christ in a spiritual manner until he comes

positions.statement: Believers truly receive Christ's body and blood in the Supper, but spiritually and by faith; the body is not in or under the bread, and unbelievers receive only the outward signs.
positions.mark: The passage says Christ's body is received only spiritually or by faith (not by the mouth), or that unbelievers who eat receive the sign but not the body.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says the bread itself is or contains the body so that the mouth receives it, or that unbelievers also receive the body; or that nothing is received but a reminder.
positions.first_defined: Consensus Tigurinus (1549); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)
positions.notes: Anglican teaching varies; Article XXVIII is the formal text. Methodist articles omit the Anglican clause that unbelievers receive only the outward signs.

positions.name: Sacramental union

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article X (1530)
defined.quote: Of the Supper of the Lord they teach that the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat the Supper of the Lord

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration VII.35 (1577)
defined.quote: under the bread, with the bread, in the bread [the body of Christ is present and offered], are employed, is that by means of them the papistical transubstantiation may be rejected and the sacramental union of the unchanged essence of the bread and of the body of Christ indicated

positions.statement: Christ's true body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine in their essence, and are received by the mouth by all who eat, worthy or unworthy.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread remains bread (keeps its nature or substance) while Christ's true body is present with it or given with it.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says the bread's nature is changed so that it no longer remains bread; or that the body is received only by faith; or only symbolized.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession, Article X (1530); Formula of Concord, Article VII (1577)
positions.notes: Lutherans reject the outsider's label 'consubstantiation'. The Orthodox Synod of Jerusalem (1672, Decree 17) rejects Lutheran 'impanation'.

positions.name: Real change, manner undefined

defined.source: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, Epiclesis
defined.quote: And make this bread the precious Body of Your Christ. ... And that which is in this cup the precious Blood of Your Christ. ... Changing them by Your Holy Spirit.

defined.source: Longer Catechism of St Philaret of Moscow, q. 340 (1830s)
defined.quote: the word transubstantiation is not to be taken to define the manner in which the bread and wine are changed into the Body and Blood of the Lord; for this none can understand but God

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1375
defined.quote: It is by the conversion of the bread and wine into Christ's body and blood that Christ becomes present in this sacrament.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: During the service of the Holy Liturgy, the bread turns into the true flesh of the Son of God and the wine into the true blood of the Son of God.

defined.source: Assyrian Church of the East, Diocese of California, FAQ
defined.quote: The elements of bread and wine are transformed in the eucharistic prayer, in a mystical way, by the unseen action of the Holy Spirit who operates through the priest celebrating this most sacred action.

positions.statement: By God's action at the consecration the bread and wine are changed into, and become, Christ's body and blood, so that they are no longer simply bread and wine; how the change happens is not defined.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread and wine are changed, transformed or made into Christ's body and blood (a change in what they are), without saying how.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says the bread keeps its own nature as bread after the consecration, or that it is only a sign, or that the body is received only by faith.
positions.first_defined: Prayed in the eastern epiclesis; stated by the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) and, for Catholics, Lateran IV (1215) and Trent (1551)
positions.notes: Catholics hold this together with transubstantiation, which specifies the manner. Oriental Orthodox placement rests on the Ethiopian text (the Armenian page says only that Christ is present).

positions.name: Transubstantiation

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 13, Canon 2 (1551)
defined.quote: that wonderful and singular conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the Body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the Blood-the species Only of the bread and wine remaining-which conversion indeed the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 13, ch. 1 (1551)
defined.quote: He be, in many other places, sacramentally present to us in his own substance, by a manner of existing, which, though we can scarcely express it in words

positions.statement: The whole substance of the bread and wine is converted into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the appearances (everything the senses or any physical test can detect) remain; so the change is not physical or chemical.
positions.mark: The passage distinguishes what the bread is (now Christ's body) from what it still appears to be to the senses (bread), saying the appearance remains while the reality is changed.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says the bread's nature or substance remains after consecration, or that the change is visible or physical, or denies any change.
positions.first_defined: Fourth Lateran Council (1215); Council of Trent, Session 13 (1551)
positions.notes: The Orthodox Synod of Jerusalem (1672) used the word, but Philaret's catechism denies that it defines the manner; Orthodoxy is in neither list.

rejected_by_sources.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
rejected_by_sources.quote: Transubstantiation, or the change of the substance of bread and wine in the Supper of our Lord, cannot be proved by Holy Writ, but is repugnant to the plain words of Scripture

shared_ground: 'This is my body' and 'this is my blood' quoted or affirmed (excludes memorial, decides nothing among the other four)
Christ's body and blood are truly given or received in the Supper (shared by spiritual presence, sacramental union, real change, transubstantiation)
Calling the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ, or the bread of life (all realist positions)
The Supper must be received worthily; unworthy eating brings judgment
The Supper is done in remembrance of Christ's death (all five positions)
Christ's body is in heaven at the Father's right hand (all positions affirm the ascension)
queries: the bread becomes the body of Christ
symbol of the body and blood
it is not bread though it seems bread
eat the flesh of Christ by faith
changed into the body and blood
notes: Hard: early writers often move between realist and figure language in one passage; only the mark decides a position.

tradition_notes.note: Divided. The Schleitheim (1527) and Dordrecht (1632) confessions keep the Supper in remembrance; the 1995 Mennonite Confession says the gathered body of believers shares in the body and blood of Christ.

question: Is the Eucharist a sacrifice, and if so, of what kind?

positions.name: Not a sacrifice

defined.source: Huldrych Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles, Article 18 (1523)
defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

positions.statement: The Supper is a remembrance of Christ's once-for-all sacrifice and is not itself a sacrifice in any sense.
positions.mark: The passage says the Supper is not a sacrifice at all, only a remembrance.
positions.excluded_by: The passage calls the Eucharist itself a sacrifice or offering made to God, of any kind.
positions.first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523)

positions.name: Sacrifice of praise and commemoration only

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXIV.19 (1531)
defined.quote: The other species is the eucharistic sacrifice, which does not merit the remission of sins or reconciliation, but is rendered by those who have been reconciled, in order that we may give thanks

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 29.2 (1646)
defined.quote: In this sacrament, Christ is not offered up to his Father; nor any real sacrifice made at all, for remission of sins of the quick or dead; but only a commemoration of that one offering up of himself

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXXI (1571)
defined.quote: Wherefore the sacrifices of Masses, in the which it was commonly said, that the Priest did offer Christ for the quick and the dead, to have remission of pain or guilt, were blasphemous fables

positions.statement: The Supper includes a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving and commemorates Christ's sacrifice, but Christ is not offered to God in it and it obtains no forgiveness for the living or the dead.
positions.mark: The passage limits the Eucharistic offering to praise, thanksgiving or remembrance, denying that Christ is offered or that it obtains forgiveness for anyone.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Christ himself is offered to God in the Eucharist, or that it is offered to obtain forgiveness or help for the living or the dead.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession XXIV and Apology XXIV (1530-31); Thirty-Nine Articles XXXI (1563/71); Westminster 29.2 (1646)

positions.name: Propitiatory sacrifice

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 22, ch. 2 (1562)
defined.quote: that same Christ is contained and immolated in an unbloody manner, who once offered Himself in a bloody manner on the altar of the cross

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 17 (1672)
defined.quote: it is a true and propitiatory Sacrifice offered for all Orthodox, living and dead

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1367
defined.quote: The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice

defined.source: CopticChurch.net, Sacraments: Eucharist
defined.quote: Be well knowledgeable of the sublime value of the sacrifice between your hands. He is Christ Emmanuel who sacrificed Himself for you.

positions.statement: In the Eucharist the one sacrifice of Christ is offered to God without bloodshed, and it obtains mercy and forgiveness for the living and the dead.
positions.mark: The passage says the Eucharist is offered for sins, or for the living and the dead to obtain mercy, or that Christ (his body and blood) is the victim offered in it.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says nothing is offered in the Supper except praise and thanksgiving, or that it profits no one but the communicant.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 22 (1562); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)

rejected_by_sources.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
rejected_by_sources.quote: The offering of Christ, once made, is that perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction for all the sins of the whole world, both original and actual; and there is none other satisfaction for sin but that alone.

positions.notes: Oriental Orthodox placement rests on Coptic and Ethiopian texts.

shared_ground: Christ's sacrifice on the cross was once for all and complete (all positions affirm this)
The Supper remembers or proclaims Christ's death
Thanksgiving and praise are offered at the Eucharist (praise and propitiatory positions both affirm it)
Calling the Eucharist an 'offering' or 'sacrifice' with no statement of what is offered or for what purpose (decides between no-sacrifice and the others only)
Malachi 1:11 'pure offering' applied to Christian worship without further specification
queries: the priest offers the body of Christ
propitiation for the living and the dead
the one sacrifice once for all
notes: Hard: 'sacrifice' and 'offering' are everywhere in early liturgy; only a purpose (forgiveness, the dead) or a named victim (Christ) decides for the propitiatory position.

question: What authority does the bishop of Rome hold over the whole Church?

positions.name: No special authority

defined.source: Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope, 9 (1537)
defined.quote: Christ sends forth His disciples on an equality, without any distinction

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXXVII (1571)
defined.quote: The Bishop of Rome hath no jurisdiction in this Realm of England

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 26.4 (1689)
defined.quote: neither can the Pope of Rome in any sense be head thereof

positions.statement: The bishop of Rome holds no authority or rank over other churches by divine institution; all ministers are equal.
positions.mark: The passage says the apostles or bishops are all equal and that none, including Rome's, holds a God-given rank or authority over others.
positions.excluded_by: The passage gives Rome or Peter's successor a rank or authority over other churches, whether of honour or of jurisdiction.
positions.first_defined: Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope (1537); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571)
positions.notes: Melanchthon signed the Smalcald Articles with the reservation that the pope's superiority could be conceded 'by human right'; that fits 'primacy-of-honour'.

positions.name: Primacy of honour among equals

defined.source: Moscow Patriarchate, Position on the problem of primacy in the Universal Church (2013)
defined.quote: In the first millennium of church history, the primacy of honour used to belong to the chair of Rome.

defined.source: Moscow Patriarchate, Position on the problem of primacy in the Universal Church (2013)
defined.quote: They also believed that primacy in honour accorded to the bishops of Rome is instituted not by God but men.

positions.statement: Rome held first place in honour among the churches, granted by the Church and not by divine right, without jurisdiction over other local churches.
positions.mark: The passage gives Rome first rank or precedence while denying it jurisdiction over other churches, or grounds its rank in councils or the city rather than in Christ's grant to Peter.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Rome's bishop holds, by Christ's institution, authority to govern or judge other churches; or denies Rome any precedence.
positions.first_defined: Councils of Constantinople (381, canon 3) and Chalcedon (451, canon 28) on the order of sees; Moscow Patriarchate statement (2013)

positions.name: Primacy of jurisdiction by divine right

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 2 (1870)
defined.quote: Therefore whoever succeeds to the chair of Peter obtains by the institution of Christ himself, the primacy of Peter over the whole church.

defined.source: Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli (1439)
defined.quote: to him was committed in blessed Peter the full power of tending, ruling and governing the whole church

positions.statement: By Christ's institution, the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor holds full and immediate power to govern the whole Church.
positions.mark: The passage says Rome's bishop, as Peter's successor, has authority (not only honour) over all churches, such as to judge, depose or bind other bishops, by Christ's grant.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Rome's rank is only of honour, or comes only from councils or the city's status, or that other bishops are not subject to it.
positions.first_defined: Council of Florence (1439); First Vatican Council (1870)

rejected_by_sources.source: Assyrian Church of the East, Diocese of California, FAQ
rejected_by_sources.quote: It is an independent patriarchate, not subject to the Bishop of Rome, or any other patriarchate.

positions.name: Infallibility of solemn papal definitions

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: when the Roman pontiff speaks EX CATHEDRA, that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church, he possesses ... that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his church to enjoy

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: such definitions of the Roman pontiff are of themselves, and not by the consent of the church, irreformable.

positions.statement: When the bishop of Rome solemnly defines a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church, he cannot err, and the definition binds without the Church's later consent.
positions.mark: The passage says a Roman bishop's doctrinal decision cannot be in error, or is final in itself without needing a council's or the churches' acceptance.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says a Roman bishop erred in faith, or that his doctrinal decisions need confirmation by a council or the churches.
positions.first_defined: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
positions.notes: Builds on primacy-of-jurisdiction: a passage stating infallibility also states the jurisdiction mark.

shared_ground: Peter was a leading apostle, named first in the lists
Peter and Paul taught and died in Rome; Rome is an apostolic church
Rome is an important church whose faith is praised
Communion between churches, including with Rome, matters
Bishops succeed the apostles in their sees
queries: the church of the Romans presides
first place of honour after Rome
appeal to the bishop of Rome
because Rome is the imperial city
notes: Hard: early praise of Rome (Ignatius 'presides in love', Irenaeus 'more powerful origin') fits both honour and jurisdiction; graders should mark it compatible unless it speaks of authority to govern or judge.

question: May Mary be called Mother of God (Theotokos)?

positions.name: Mother of God (Theotokos)

defined.source: Council of Ephesus, Cyril's First Anathema (431)
defined.quote: If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is God in truth, and therefore that the holy virgin is the mother of God

defined.source: Council of Chalcedon, Definition of Faith (451)
defined.quote: in the last days the same for us and for our salvation from Mary, the virgin God-bearer as regards his humanity

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), The Holy Virgin Saint Mary
defined.quote: She is, in the belief of the Church, the mother of God, (Theotokos in Coptic)

positions.statement: Because the one born of Mary is God the Word made flesh, Mary is rightly called Mother of God.
positions.mark: The passage calls Mary Mother of God or God-bearer, or says God was born of her.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Mary should be called mother of Christ but not Mother of God, or that she bore only a man joined to God.
positions.first_defined: Council of Ephesus (431); Council of Chalcedon (451)
positions.notes: All traditions here receive Chalcedon; in devotion the title is mainly Catholic and Orthodox.

positions.name: Mother of Christ only
positions.statement: Mary should be called mother of Christ, not Mother of God, because she bore the humanity, not the Godhead.
positions.mark: The passage refuses the title Mother of God, preferring mother of Christ or of the man.
positions.excluded_by: The passage calls Mary Mother of God or says God was born of her.
positions.first_defined: Condemned at Ephesus (431)
positions.notes: No present tradition here holds it; kept so graders can record early writers (e.g. Nestorius) who did.
positions.defined_status: unverified: no official defining text found and fetched

shared_ground: Mary is the mother of Jesus
Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit of the virgin Mary
Mary did not give the Word his divine nature
queries: God was born of the virgin
mother of Christ not of God

tradition_notes.note: Not placed. It prays to Mary as 'the Mother of Christ our God and Saviour'; in 1994 it recognised with Rome 'the legitimacy and rightness' of calling her Mother of God. Before then it refused the title.

question: Did Mary remain a virgin all her life?

positions.name: Perpetual virginity

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 499
defined.quote: The deepening of faith in the virginal motherhood led the Church to confess Mary's real and perpetual virginity even in the act of giving birth to the Son of God made man.

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 7 (1672)
defined.quote: being conceived of the Holy Spirit, in the womb of the ever-virgin Mary

defined.source: Kontakion of the Dormition (Orthodox Church in America)
defined.quote: she was translated into life by Him who dwelt in her ever-virginal womb.

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), The Holy Virgin Saint Mary
defined.quote: The Church believes in the perpetuality of the virginity of The Virgin.

positions.statement: Mary remained a virgin before, in and after Jesus' birth, and had no other children.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary stayed a virgin after Jesus' birth, or calls her ever-virgin, or says the Lord's brothers were not her children.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Mary had children with Joseph after Jesus' birth.
positions.first_defined: 'Ever-virgin' at the Second Council of Constantinople (553); Lateran Synod (649)
positions.notes: Luther and early Reformers held it; no Protestant confession here rejects it.

positions.name: Mary had other children
positions.statement: After Jesus' birth Mary and Joseph lived as married and had other children, the Lord's brothers and sisters.
positions.mark: The passage says the Lord's brothers were Mary's own sons, or that she did not remain a virgin after Jesus' birth.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Mary remained a virgin all her life.
positions.first_defined: No confession defines it
positions.notes: Held by many modern Protestants without a confessional text; kept so graders can record early writers (e.g. Helvidius, as reported) who held it.
positions.defined_status: unverified: no official defining text found and fetched

shared_ground: Mary conceived Jesus as a virgin (virginal conception)
Mary is called 'the Virgin' as a title in connection with Christ's birth
queries: Joseph's sons by a former wife
until she brought forth her firstborn

question: Was Mary free from sin, and from when?

positions.name: Mary had personal faults
positions.statement: Mary, though holy, committed some personal faults, such as doubt or vanity, like other believers.
positions.mark: The passage attributes a sin, fault, doubt or weakness to Mary.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Mary never sinned.
positions.first_defined: No confession defines it
positions.notes: No tradition here defines it; kept because several early writers attribute faults to Mary.
positions.defined_status: unverified: no official defining text found and fetched

positions.name: Free from personal sin

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 6, Canon 23 (1547)
defined.quote: except by a special privilege from God, as the Church holds in regard of the Blessed Virgin

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 6 (1672)
defined.quote: and especially the Mother of God the Word, the ever-virgin Mary, did not experience these [sins], or such like faults.

positions.statement: Mary never committed any personal sin during her life, by a special grace of God.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary committed no sin, or was wholly pure in her life, without saying anything about her conception.
positions.excluded_by: The passage attributes any sin or fault to Mary.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 6, Canon 23 (1547); Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 6 (1672)
positions.notes: Dositheus groups Mary with the Forerunner and prophets as free from grave actual sins, so its claim is weaker than Trent's.

positions.name: Immaculate Conception

defined.source: Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854)
defined.quote: the most Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instance of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege granted by Almighty God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, was preserved free from all stain of original sin

positions.statement: From the first moment of her conception Mary was preserved from original sin, by a grace given in view of Christ's merits.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary was without original sin, or holy from her conception, not only free from personal sin.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Mary was conceived in original sin, or was cleansed of sin only later (e.g. at the Annunciation).
positions.first_defined: Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854)
positions.notes: Widely rejected by Orthodox and Protestant writers, but no council of theirs condemns it by name.

shared_ground: Mary is holy, blessed, highly favoured
Mary as the new Eve, obedient where Eve disobeyed
Mary needed and received God's grace
queries: the sword that pierced Mary's soul
Mary cleansed by the Holy Spirit
Christ alone was born without sin
notes: Hard: early praise of Mary as 'spotless' or 'all-holy' usually states personal sinlessness at most; only a statement about her conception states the Immaculate Conception mark.

tradition_notes.note: Not placed. Pope Shenouda III (Coptic) rejects the Immaculate Conception; Ethiopian, Armenian and Syriac teaching has not been checked yet.

question: How did Mary's earthly life end?

positions.name: Died and was buried; nothing further held
positions.statement: Mary died and was buried like other believers, and awaits the general resurrection.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary's body lies in the grave or awaits the general resurrection, or that her end is unknown.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Mary's body was taken into heaven.
positions.first_defined: No confession defines it
positions.notes: Protestant confessions are silent; kept so graders can record early writers (e.g. Epiphanius) who say her end is unknown.
positions.defined_status: unverified: no official defining text found and fetched

positions.name: Died, then taken bodily to heaven (Dormition)

defined.source: Troparion and Kontakion of the Dormition (Orthodox Church in America)
defined.quote: in falling asleep you did not forsake the world, O Theotokos.

defined.source: Kontakion of the Dormition (Orthodox Church in America)
defined.quote: Neither the tomb, nor death had power over the Theotokos

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), The Holy Virgin Saint Mary
defined.quote: The Church believes in the Ascent of the body of The Virgin to heaven, and celebrates that feast on the 16th of Misra.

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), The Holy Virgin Saint Mary
defined.quote: in commemoration of her death on the 21st of Tubah

positions.statement: Mary truly died (fell asleep), and was then raised and taken into heavenly life; neither tomb nor death held her.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary died and that afterwards her body did not remain in the tomb, or that she was raised.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Mary's body remains buried, or that she did not die at all.
positions.first_defined: Liturgical feast of the Dormition (from the 6th century); not defined as dogma
positions.notes: Held in Orthodox liturgy, not as defined dogma. Oriental Orthodox placement rests on the Coptic text only.

positions.name: Assumed body and soul (Catholic dogma)

defined.source: Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus, 44 (1950)
defined.quote: that the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory.

positions.statement: At the end of her earthly life Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory; the dogma leaves open whether she first died.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary was taken body and soul into heaven.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says Mary's body remains in the grave or is venerated as a relic.
positions.first_defined: Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus (1950)
positions.notes: Hard: the bodily assumption is also the Orthodox belief; any passage stating it states both 'assumption' and 'dormition' unless it denies her death.

shared_ground: Mary's earthly life came to an end
Mary is honoured in heaven
Mary's 'falling asleep' named without saying what happened to her body (fits all three)
queries: falling asleep of the Mother of God
Mary's body taken up into heaven
no one knows the end of Mary
Mary's body did not see corruption

question: What is the relationship between Christians on earth and the saints in heaven?

positions.name: Remembered as examples only

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 21.2 (1646)
defined.quote: Religious worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; and to him alone; not to angels, saints, or any other creature

positions.statement: The saints are remembered as examples of faith; no claim is made that they pray for us, and they are not to be addressed in prayer.
positions.mark: The passage says prayer is to be made to God alone and never to departed saints, without saying the saints pray for us.
positions.excluded_by: The passage asks a departed saint for prayer or help, or says departed saints pray for the living.
positions.first_defined: Westminster Confession, 21.2 (1646)

positions.name: The saints pray for the Church, but are not to be invoked

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXI.9 (1531)
defined.quote: concerning the saints we concede that, just as, when alive, they pray for the Church universal in general, so in heaven they pray for the Church in general

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article XXI (1530)
defined.quote: But the Scripture teaches not the invocation of saints or to ask help of saints, since it sets before us the one Christ as the Mediator

positions.statement: The saints in heaven pray for the Church in general, but Christians should not call on them or ask their help.
positions.mark: The passage says departed saints pray for the Church while denying that Christians should address them.
positions.excluded_by: The passage directly asks a departed saint for prayer or help; or denies that the saints pray for the Church.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession XXI (1530); Apology XXI (1531)

positions.name: Asking the saints to pray for us

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, On the invocation of saints (1563)
defined.quote: the saints, who reign together with Christ, offer up their own prayers to God for men; that it is good and useful suppliantly to invoke them

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 8 (1672)
defined.quote: Notwithstanding, in [our] prayers and supplications unto Him, we say the Saints are intercessors, and, above all, the undefiled Mother of the very God the Word

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), Comparative Theology (1988)
defined.quote: We reply that we do not pray to the saints; we only ask their prayers and their support for us.

positions.statement: Departed saints pray for the living, and it is right to address them directly and ask for their prayers.
positions.mark: The passage addresses a departed saint directly (such as 'pray for us') or teaches that Christians should ask departed saints for their prayers.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says prayer must never be addressed to a departed saint.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 25 (1563); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)
positions.notes: Anglican Article XXII rejects 'invocation of Saints'. Oriental Orthodox placement rests on Coptic texts.

rejected_by_sources.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
rejected_by_sources.quote: The Romish doctrine concerning purgatory, pardon, worshiping, and adoration, as well of images as of relics, and also invocation of saints, is … grounded upon no warrant of Scripture, but repugnant to the Word of God.

shared_ground: The saints are honoured and remembered as examples of faith (Augsburg XXI: 'the memory of saints may be set before us')
Living Christians should pray for one another
Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity
Feasts or remembrance of martyrs on their days
queries: do the dead know what happens here
the saints pray for the church
prayer at the tomb of the martyr
notes: Hard: early epitaphs and inscriptions asking the dead to pray are invocation; a homily saying the martyrs pray for us states only 'pray-but-not-invoked' or is compatible with 'invocation'.

question: Is Scripture the only infallible rule of faith, or is Church tradition also binding?

positions.name: Scripture the only infallible rule

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm, 1 (1577)
defined.quote: the sole rule and standard according to which all dogmas together with [all] teachers should be estimated and judged are the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and of the New Testament alone

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 1.10 (1646)
defined.quote: The supreme judge by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article VI (1571)
defined.quote: Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation: so that whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man, that it should be believed as an article of the Faith

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: The Bible is our all-sufficient rule for faith and practice.

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation; so that whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man that it should be believed as an article of faith

defined.source: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995)
defined.quote: Other claims on our understanding of Christian faith and life, such as tradition, culture, experience, reason, and political powers, need to be tested and corrected by the light of Holy Scripture.

positions.statement: Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith; councils, fathers and traditions are judged by it, and nothing not provable from it may be required as necessary belief.
positions.mark: The passage says nothing may be believed as necessary unless proved from Scripture, or that councils and church teachers are to be judged by Scripture as the final norm.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says some necessary doctrine is known from unwritten tradition rather than Scripture, or that the Church's judgment binds equally with Scripture.
positions.first_defined: Formula of Concord (1577); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Scripture with binding Church tradition

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 4 (1546)
defined.quote: receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety, and reverence, all the books both of the Old and of the New Testament ... as also the said traditions, as well those appertaining to faith as to morals

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 2 (1672)
defined.quote: the witness also of the Catholic Church is, we believe, not of inferior authority to that of the Divine Scriptures.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, Canonical books
defined.quote: The word of God is not contained in the Bible alone, it is to be found in tradition as well.

positions.statement: Unwritten apostolic tradition, kept in the Church, binds with the same authority as Scripture, and the Church's interpretation of Scripture is authoritative.
positions.mark: The passage says some practice or doctrine is held from unwritten apostolic tradition with binding force, or that the Church's tradition holds equal authority with Scripture.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says nothing beyond what Scripture teaches may be required as belief.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 4 (1546); Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 2 (1672)
positions.notes: Merged Catholic and Orthodox views: Trent speaks of two channels (books and traditions) and Dositheus of the Church's equal witness. Early texts cannot tell these apart. Oriental Orthodox placement rests on Ethiopian and Coptic texts.

shared_ground: Scripture is inspired by God and true
Scripture is sufficient to refute heretics or to teach the faith (praise of Scripture alone decides nothing)
Heretics misinterpret Scripture
The 'rule of faith' or creed summarizes apostolic teaching
Church teachers and councils are to be respected
queries: we received this from the fathers not from scripture
the church is the pillar and ground of truth
notes: Hard: many early writers praise Scripture as sufficient and also appeal to unwritten customs; graders must look for a claim about the final norm, not praise.

question: Which books belong to the Old Testament?

positions.name: Hebrew canon only

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 1.3 (1646)
defined.quote: The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The names of the canonical books are: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, The First Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, The First Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, The First Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Book of Ezra, The Book of Nehemiah, The Book of Esther, The Book of Job, The Psalms, The Proverbs, Ecclesiastes or the Preacher, Cantica or Songs of Solomon, Four Prophets the Greater, Twelve Prophets the Less.

defined.source: Church of the Nazarene, Articles of Faith (Manual 2023)
defined.quote: by which we understand the 66 books of the Old and New Testaments

positions.statement: The Old Testament consists only of the books of the Hebrew canon; the others are not inspired.
positions.mark: The passage limits the Old Testament to the Hebrew books (such as a count of 22 or 24 books) and puts Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit, Judith and Maccabees outside Scripture.
positions.excluded_by: The passage counts any of those books as Scripture equal to the rest.
positions.first_defined: Westminster Confession (1646)
positions.notes: Wesley dropped the Anglican list of books read 'for example of life'.

positions.name: Read for example of life, not for doctrine

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article VI (1571)
defined.quote: And the other Books (as Hierome saith) the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine

positions.statement: The extra books are read in church for example and instruction, but are not used to establish doctrine.
positions.mark: The passage says these books are read in church or to learners but are not used to prove doctrine.
positions.excluded_by: The passage uses one of these books to prove doctrine as Scripture, or forbids reading them.
positions.first_defined: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article VI (1563/1571)
positions.notes: Lutheran Bibles print these books separately, but no Lutheran confession defines the canon.

positions.name: Wider canon as full Scripture

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 4 (1546)
defined.quote: Tobias, Judith, Esther, Job, the Davidical Psalter, consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms; the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Canticle of Canticles, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Question 3 (1672)
defined.quote: For we judge these also to be with the other genuine Books of Divine Scripture genuine parts of Scripture.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, Canonical books
defined.quote: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church has 46 books of the Old Testament and 35 books of the New Testament that will bring the total of canonized books of the Bible to 81.

positions.statement: Books such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and Maccabees are inspired Scripture on the same footing as the rest.
positions.mark: The passage lists these books among the canonical Scriptures, or cites them with full scriptural authority to prove doctrine.
positions.excluded_by: The passage excludes them from the canon or from proving doctrine.
positions.first_defined: Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397), local; Council of Trent (1546); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)
positions.notes: Orthodox canons are somewhat wider than the Catholic one (e.g. 3 Maccabees). Only the Ethiopian list was checked; Coptic, Armenian and Syriac canons also go beyond the Hebrew books but differ from each other.

shared_ground: The books of the Hebrew canon are Scripture (all positions)
The 27 books of the New Testament are Scripture (all positions)
Quoting Wisdom or Sirach as wise or edifying without calling it Scripture
queries: as it is written in Wisdom
the twenty-two books of the Hebrews
the books of the Old Testament
notes: Canon merged into Scripture-authority family as its own question because the positions differ only on the Old Testament; the New Testament is shared ground.

question: On what basis is a sinner justified before God?

positions.name: By faith alone, with Christ's righteousness imputed

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Epitome, III.2 (1577)
defined.quote: that God forgives us our sins out of pure grace, without any work, merit, or worthiness of ours preceding, present, or following, that He presents and imputes to us the righteousness of Christ's obedience

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 11.1 (1646)
defined.quote: not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XI (1571)
defined.quote: We are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ by Faith, and not for our own works or deservings

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: We are accounted righteous before God only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, by faith, and not for our own works or deservings.

positions.statement: God declares the sinner righteous by crediting Christ's righteousness to him, received by faith alone; inner renewal follows but is not the ground.
positions.mark: The passage says justification is God's verdict counting the sinner righteous on account of Christ's righteousness reckoned to him, received by faith without works.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says we are justified by a righteousness worked inside us, or by faith together with works or love.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession IV (1530); Formula of Concord III (1577); Westminster Confession 11 (1646)

rejected_by_sources.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), Comparative Theology (1988)
rejected_by_sources.quote: The Lord did not say: "He who believes is saved", but He put the condition of baptism alongside the condition of belief.

positions.name: By faith working through love, with righteousness infused

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 7 (1547)
defined.quote: the charity of God is poured forth, by the Holy Spirit, in the hearts of those that are justified, and is inherent therein

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 13 (1672)
defined.quote: We believe a man to be not simply justified through faith alone, but through faith which works through love, that is to say, through faith and works.

positions.statement: In justification God makes the sinner inwardly righteous by grace and love poured into the heart; faith justifies as faith working through love, together with works.
positions.mark: The passage says the justified are made righteous by grace or love dwelling in them, or that faith justifies together with love or works.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says justification is only a verdict that counts us righteous by Christ's righteousness reckoned to us, by faith alone.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547); Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 13 (1672)

positions.name: Salvation as union with God (theosis)
positions.statement: Salvation is the healing and deification of the person through participation in God's life, by grace and human cooperation; 'justification' is one aspect of that union.
positions.mark: The passage describes salvation as becoming god by grace or sharing in the divine nature, and treats this, not a legal verdict, as what saving righteousness is.
positions.excluded_by: The passage defines salvation as a legal verdict only, with union with God as a separate, later matter.
positions.first_defined: No conciliar definition; a frame of Orthodox theology
positions.notes: Unverified: no official Orthodox defining text was found; the Synod of Jerusalem's own justification text sits under 'infused-righteousness'. Hard to tell from that position in early texts.
positions.defined_status: unverified: no official defining text found and fetched

shared_ground: Salvation is by God's grace and through Christ's death
Faith is necessary
Good works follow true faith
Paul's 'justified by faith, not by works of the Law' quoted without further claim
Becoming partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4) quoted without saying how it relates to justification
notes: Hard: early 'faith alone' language often opposes the ritual Law, not works of love; graders must look for the imputation or infusion claim.

tradition_notes.note: Not placed. The 1995 Mennonite Confession's commentary says justification 'is experienced as a covenant relationship with God', and that justification by faith and faithful obedience 'are inseparable'.

question: From whom does the Holy Spirit eternally proceed?

positions.name: From the Father as sole source

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 1 (1672)
defined.quote: the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, and consubstantial with the Father and the Son.

defined.source: Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs, 5.i (1848)
defined.quote: This novel opinion destroys the oneness from the One cause, and the diverse origin of the Persons of the Blessed Trinity

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: The Son is born of, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from, the Father.

positions.statement: The Father alone is the source and cause of the Spirit's eternal being; the Son is not a co-cause of the Spirit.
positions.mark: The passage says the Father alone is the cause or source of the Spirit's existence, or denies that the Spirit has his being from the Son.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says the Spirit has his eternal being from the Son as well as from the Father.
positions.first_defined: Photius (9th c.); Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848)
positions.notes: Oriental Orthodox placement rests on the Ethiopian text.

positions.name: From the Father and the Son as one principle

defined.source: Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli (1439)
defined.quote: the holy Spirit is eternally from the Father and the Son, and has his essence and his subsistent being from the Father together with the Son, and proceeds from both eternally as from one principle and a single spiration.

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 2.3 (1646)
defined.quote: the Holy Ghost eternally proceeding from the Father and the Son.

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article V (1571)
defined.quote: The Holy Ghost, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is of one substance, majesty, and glory, with the Father and the Son, very and eternal God.

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: the Holy Spirit is the one proceeding from the Father and the Son

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The Holy Ghost, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is of one substance, majesty, and glory with the Father and the Son, very and eternal God.

positions.statement: The Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son together, as from one principle.
positions.mark: The passage says the Spirit eternally proceeds from, or has his being from, both the Father and the Son.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says the Father alone is the cause of the Spirit's being.
positions.first_defined: Third Council of Toledo (589, local); Council of Lyon II (1274); Council of Florence (1439)

shared_ground: The Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26)
The Spirit proceeds 'from the Father through the Son' (claimed by both positions; never a position by itself, since no tradition here defines it as one)
The Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son or of Christ
The Son sends the Spirit into the world (temporal mission)
The Spirit is consubstantial with Father and Son
The Father is the source of the Godhead
queries: the Spirit proceeds from the Father
proceeds from the Father and the Son
from the Father through the Son
the Spirit receives from the Son
notes: Hard: 'through the Son' and 'the Spirit of the Son' are shared ground; a passage must speak of the Spirit's eternal origin to state either mark.

question: What happens between death and the final judgment to those who die in faith but not fully purified, and can the living help them?

positions.name: Purgatory

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, Decree concerning Purgatory (1563)
defined.quote: there is a Purgatory, and that the souls there detained are helped by the suffrages of the faithful, but principally by the acceptable sacrifice of the altar

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1030
defined.quote: All who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are indeed assured of their eternal salvation; but after death they undergo purification, so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven.

positions.statement: Some who die in grace undergo a temporary purification after death, involving punishment still owed for forgiven sins, and the prayers and Eucharist of the living help them.
positions.mark: The passage says saved souls are purified or punished for a time after death for sins already forgiven, before entering heaven.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says every soul goes at once to final rest or final punishment, with no cleansing between.
positions.first_defined: Council of Lyon II (1274); Council of Florence (1439); Council of Trent (1563)

rejected_by_sources.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
rejected_by_sources.quote: The Romish doctrine concerning purgatory, pardon, worshiping, and adoration, as well of images as of relics, and also invocation of saints, is … grounded upon no warrant of Scripture, but repugnant to the Word of God.

positions.name: Prayer for the dead, purification not defined

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 18 (1672)
defined.quote: are delivered by the Supreme Goodness, through the prayers of the Priests, and the good works which the relatives of each do for their Departed; especially the unbloody Sacrifice benefiting the most

defined.source: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, Anaphora
defined.quote: Again, we offer this spiritual worship for those who repose in the faith

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), Comparative Theology (1988)
defined.quote: We plead for the departed in our prayers and they intercede for us through their prayers

positions.statement: The Church prays and offers the Eucharist for the departed, who are helped by it before the final judgment, without defining a place or process of purifying punishment.
positions.mark: The passage prays or offers for the departed and says they are helped or released, without describing a purifying punishment for forgiven sins.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says prayers cannot help the dead.
positions.first_defined: Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 18 (1672)
positions.notes: Hard: Decree 18 itself speaks of punishment in Hades and release through prayers, which is close to purgatory; the Orthodox reject the Latin account of satisfaction and fire. Oriental Orthodox placement rests on a Coptic text and is moderate evidence that the departed are helped.

positions.name: No purification or help after death

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 32.1 (1646)
defined.quote: Besides these two places, for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none.

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXII (1571)
defined.quote: The Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory, Pardons, Worshipping, and Adoration, as well of Images as of Reliques, and also invocation of Saints, is a fond thing vainly invented

positions.statement: At death believers' souls go at once into God's presence; there is no purifying state after death, and prayers or offerings do not change the state of the dead.
positions.mark: The passage says there is no place or state after death besides heaven and hell, or that the living cannot help the dead.
positions.excluded_by: The passage prays for the dead expecting to help them, or describes a cleansing after death.
positions.first_defined: Thirty-Nine Articles XXII (1563/1571); Westminster Confession 32 (1646)
positions.notes: Article XXII rejects 'the Romish doctrine' of purgatory; Anglican practice on prayer for the dead varies. Lutherans reject purgatory (Smalcald Articles) but have not condemned all prayer for the dead.

shared_ground: The souls of the dead live on and await the resurrection
The faithful departed are at rest or with Christ
Remembering the departed by name at worship, without asking that they be helped
Final judgment and resurrection of the body
queries: offering for those who have fallen asleep
saved yet so as through fire
sins forgiven in the world to come
the Eucharist offered for the departed
notes: Indulgences are a separate question because they concern the Church's power, not the state of the dead.

question: Can the Church remit the temporal punishment still owed for forgiven sins?

positions.name: Indulgences

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, Decree concerning Indulgences (1563)
defined.quote: the power of conferring Indulgences was granted by Christ to the Church; and she has, even in the most ancient times, used the said power

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1471
defined.quote: An indulgence is a remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven

positions.statement: The Church has authority to remit before God temporal punishment owed for forgiven sins, drawing on the merits of Christ and the saints.
positions.mark: The passage says the Church (a bishop, or martyrs' intercession accepted by the Church) remits punishment owed before God, not only a church penalty.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says once God forgives no punishment remains, or that no one can lessen what God requires.
positions.first_defined: Clement VI, Unigenitus (1343); Council of Trent, Session 25 (1563)

positions.name: No such power

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXII (1571)
defined.quote: The Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory, Pardons, Worshipping, and Adoration, as well of Images as of Reliques, and also invocation of Saints, is a fond thing vainly invented

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The Romish doctrine concerning purgatory, pardon, worshiping, and adoration, as well of images as of relics, and also invocation of saints, is … grounded upon no warrant of Scripture, but repugnant to the Word of God.

positions.statement: The Church has no power to remit punishment before God; forgiveness through Christ leaves no punishment for the Church to lessen.
positions.mark: The passage says God's forgiveness leaves no remaining punishment, or that no church authority can lessen it.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says the Church can remit punishment owed before God.
positions.first_defined: Thirty-Nine Articles XXII (1563/1571)
positions.notes: Orthodoxy has no defined position; the practice did not develop in the East. 'Pardon' in Methodist Article XIV (from Anglican Article XXII) means indulgences.

shared_ground: Bishops may shorten or relax church penances they imposed (a church discipline, not punishment before God)
Martyrs' and confessors' intercession for the lapsed
Penance and satisfaction after baptism as church discipline
queries: relaxing the penance of the lapsed
letters of peace from the martyrs
merits of the martyrs for sinners
notes: Hard: early relaxation of penance concerns church discipline; only a claim about punishment before God states the indulgences mark.

question: Who should be baptized?

positions.name: Believers and their infants

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1250
defined.quote: Born with a fallen human nature and tainted by original sin, children also have need of the new birth in Baptism

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article IX (1530)
defined.quote: children are to be baptized who, being offered to God through Baptism are received into God's grace.

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 28.4 (1646)
defined.quote: Not only those that do actually profess faith in and obedience unto Christ, but also the infants of one, or both, believing parents, are to be baptized.

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The Baptism of young children is to be retained in the Church.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahido Church baptizes male infants at the age of 40 days and female infants at the age of 80 days

defined.source: Common Statement on Sacramental Life, Catholic Church and Assyrian Church of the East (2017)
defined.quote: both the Catholic and the Assyrian tradition practice the baptism of adults and the baptism of infants.

positions.statement: Infants of Christian parents should be baptized, before they can profess faith themselves.
positions.mark: The passage says infants or little children are, or should be, baptized.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says baptism must wait until a person can profess faith.
positions.first_defined: Council of Carthage (418); Augsburg Confession (1530); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Professing believers only

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 29.2 (1689)
defined.quote: Those who do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ, are the only proper subjects of this ordinance.

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: Christian baptism is the immersion of a believer in water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

defined.source: Schleitheim Confession (1527)
defined.quote: This excludes all infant baptism

defined.source: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995)
defined.quote: water baptism is to be reserved for those old enough to make such a pledge.

positions.statement: Only those who personally profess repentance and faith should be baptized; infants should not be.
positions.mark: The passage says only those who can profess faith should be baptized, or that infants should not be.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says infants are or should be baptized.
positions.first_defined: Schleitheim Confession (1527); First London Confession (1644); Second London Confession (1689)

shared_ground: Adults who come to faith are baptized after instruction (catechumenate)
Baptism in the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit
Repentance and faith are expected of adult candidates
Advice to delay baptism for prudential reasons (e.g. Tertullian) without saying infant baptism is invalid (compatible with both)
queries: baptism from the apostles for infants

question: What does baptism do?

positions.name: Baptism regenerates and forgives sins

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1213
defined.quote: Through Baptism we are freed from sin and reborn as sons of God; we become members of Christ, are incorporated into the Church

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article IX (1530)
defined.quote: Of Baptism they teach that it is necessary to salvation, and that through Baptism is offered the grace of God

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 16 (1672)
defined.quote: We believe Holy Baptism, which was instituted by the Lord, and is conferred in the name of the Holy Trinity, to be of the highest necessity.

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), Comparative Theology (1988)
defined.quote: Through baptism we receive the Second Birth which is of water and the Spirit

defined.source: Assyrian Church of the East, Diocese of California, FAQ
defined.quote: It is a new birth, according to water and the Holy Spirit (cf. John 3:5) without which one may not enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.

positions.statement: Baptism itself is God's means of regeneration and forgiveness of sins, and is ordinarily necessary for salvation.
positions.mark: The passage says baptism itself washes away sin, gives new birth, or is the means by which one is regenerated.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says baptism only signifies a regeneration that happened or will happen apart from it.
positions.first_defined: Council of Carthage (418); Augsburg Confession IX (1530); Council of Trent (1547)

positions.name: Sign and seal of grace, not tied to the moment

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 28.1 (1646)
defined.quote: to be unto him a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, of his ingrafting into Christ, of regeneration, of remission of sins

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 28.5-6 (1646)
defined.quote: grace and salvation are not so inseparably annexed unto it, as that no person can be regenerated, or saved, without it; or, that all that are baptized are undoubtedly regenerated. ... The efficacy of baptism is not tied to that moment of time wherein it is administered

positions.statement: Baptism signs and seals God's promise of regeneration and forgiveness and conveys that grace to the elect in God's time, but not everyone baptized is regenerated and the grace is not tied to the moment.
positions.mark: The passage says baptism seals or confirms grace while denying that all the baptized are regenerated or that regeneration happens at the moment of baptism.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says every person baptized is regenerated by it; or that it is a bare symbol conveying nothing.
positions.first_defined: Westminster Confession 28 (1646)
positions.notes: Anglican Article XXVII ('a sign of Regeneration... as by an instrument') and the Prayer Book rite read both ways; Anglicans are left in neither list.

positions.name: Symbol of faith already received

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: It is an act of obedience symbolizing the believer's faith in a crucified, buried, and risen Saviour, the believer's death to sin, the burial of the old life, and the resurrection to walk in newness of life in Christ Jesus.

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 29.1 (1689)
defined.quote: Baptism is an ordinance of the New Testament, ordained by Jesus Christ, to be unto the party baptized, a sign of his fellowship with him, in his death and resurrection

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: Thus they declare to the world that they have died with Christ and that they also have been raised with Him to walk in newness of life.

defined.source: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995)
defined.quote: Baptism by water is a sign that a person has repented, received forgiveness, renounced evil, and died to sin

positions.statement: Baptism is an act of obedience by one already saved, picturing the faith and new life already received; it is not a means of regeneration.
positions.mark: The passage says baptism pictures or testifies to a salvation already received, and does not itself convey grace.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says baptism washes away sin or gives new birth.
positions.first_defined: First London Confession (1644); Baptist Faith and Message (1925/2000)

shared_ground: Baptism is commanded by Christ
Baptism is linked with repentance, forgiveness and new life (Acts 2:38) in quoting Scripture
Baptism joins a person to the visible church
Faith is required of adult candidates
queries: born again of water and the Spirit
the baptized who are not reborn
notes: Split from baptism-subjects because the texts answer the two questions separately (e.g. Reformed baptize infants but deny automatic regeneration).

tradition_notes.note: Divided. Article XVII calls baptism 'a sign of regeneration or the new birth', which can be read either way; John Wesley affirmed 'the regenerating grace of infant baptism'.

question: How is the Church governed, and who ordains its ministers?

positions.name: Bishops in apostolic succession

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 77
defined.quote: In order that the full and living Gospel might always be preserved in the Church the apostles left bishops as their successors.

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 10 (1672)
defined.quote: he, as a successor of the Apostles, having received in continued succession by the imposition of hands and the invocation of the All-holy Spirit the grace that is given him of the Lord of binding and loosing

defined.source: Book of Common Prayer, Preface to the Ordinal (1662)
defined.quote: It is evident unto all men diligently reading holy Scripture and ancient Authors, that from the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of Ministers in Christ's Church; Bishops, Priests, and Deacons.

defined.source: CopticChurch.net, Sacraments: Priesthood
defined.quote: the service of Patriarchs, successors of the Apostles everywhere, at all times

defined.source: Common Statement on Sacramental Life, Catholic Church and Assyrian Church of the East (2017)
defined.quote: The requirement that all ordained ministers of the Church should stand in the apostolic succession, in virtue of their sacramental ordination, is an expression and a guarantee of continuity between the apostolic origin of the Church and the present qualification of her ministers.

positions.statement: Bishops, distinct from and above presbyters, succeed the apostles through an unbroken line of ordination, and govern the churches.
positions.mark: The passage places one bishop over presbyters and deacons as successor of the apostles, or traces bishops in a line from the apostles.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says bishop and presbyter are one and the same office, or that a congregation may ordain without a bishop.
positions.first_defined: Not a single dogma; Council of Trent, Session 23 (1563); Anglican Ordinal (1550/1662); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)
positions.notes: Lutherans vary; some kept episcopal succession, so they are in neither list.

positions.name: Equal presbyters governing in councils

defined.source: Belgic Confession, Article 31 (1561)
defined.quote: As for the ministers of the Word, they all have the same power and authority, no matter where they may be

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 31.1 (1646)
defined.quote: For the better government, and further edification of the church, there ought to be such assemblies as are commonly called synods or councils

positions.statement: All ministers of the Word hold equal authority; churches are governed by elders, and congregations are joined under assemblies of elders (synods).
positions.mark: The passage says presbyters and bishops are equal in authority, or that churches are governed jointly by a body of elders above the congregation.
positions.excluded_by: The passage puts one bishop above the presbyters by divine institution; or makes each congregation fully self-governing.
positions.first_defined: Belgic Confession (1561); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Self-governing congregation

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 26.7 (1689)
defined.quote: To each of these churches thus gathered, according to his mind declared in his word, he hath given all that power and authority, which is in any way needful for their carrying on that order in worship and discipline

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VI (2000)
defined.quote: A New Testament church of the Lord Jesus Christ is an autonomous local congregation of baptized believers, associated by covenant in the faith and fellowship of the gospel

positions.statement: Each gathered congregation holds full authority from Christ to choose its officers and exercise discipline, with no higher church body over it.
positions.mark: The passage says a local congregation holds full authority in itself, with no bishop or synod above it.
positions.excluded_by: The passage puts a bishop or synod in authority over local congregations.
positions.first_defined: Cambridge Platform (1648); Second London Baptist Confession, ch. 26 (1689)

shared_ground: There are ordained ministers called elders or presbyters, and deacons
Ordination by laying on of hands with prayer
The congregation has a part in choosing or approving its ministers
Church discipline is exercised
Councils of bishops met to settle disputes (as a historical fact, without a claim about divine institution)
queries: bishop and presbyter are the same
succession of bishops from the apostles
chosen by the vote of the people
notes: Hard: Jerome and others say bishop and presbyter were once one office; that states the presbyterian mark only if it also denies the bishop's present authority.

tradition_notes.note: Divided. United Methodist bishops are not ordained as bishops but are clergy 'elected and consecrated to the office of bishop'; Methodist churches in the British line have no bishops.
Divided. Mennonite conferences describe both congregation-first and conference-first polity; Amish and Old Order bishops are chosen by lot.
Divided. The Assemblies of God mixes congregational and presbyterian features; the Church of God (Cleveland) and COGIC have strong central or episcopal offices.

question: May images of Christ and the saints be made, and should they be honoured?

positions.name: Images venerated

defined.source: Second Council of Nicaea, Definition (787)
defined.quote: the honour paid to an image traverses it, reaching the model, and he who venerates the image, venerates the person represented in that image.

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Question 4 (1672)
defined.quote: the honor paid to the Icon is not at all divided or at all different from [the honor paid to the one who] is portrayed

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), Comparative Theology (1988)
defined.quote: venerating icons, kissing them, lighting candles in front of them and kneeling before them. We will try to reply to all these points, showing the spiritual benefits of icons and why the Church keeps them.

positions.statement: Images of Christ, Mary and the saints should be set up and honoured with outward signs (kissing, bowing, lights, incense); the honour passes to the person shown and differs from the worship due to God.
positions.mark: The passage approves honouring an image with outward acts (kissing, bowing, lights, incense), or says honour given to an image passes to the person shown.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says honouring or bowing to any image is wrong, or that images must not be in churches.
positions.first_defined: Second Council of Nicaea (787)

rejected_by_sources.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
rejected_by_sources.quote: The Romish doctrine concerning purgatory, pardon, worshiping, and adoration, as well of images as of relics, and also invocation of saints, is … grounded upon no warrant of Scripture, but repugnant to the Word of God.

positions.notes: Oriental Orthodox placement rests on a Coptic text; Armenian churches use fewer icons.

positions.name: Images allowed as adornment, not venerated

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXIV.51 (1531)
defined.quote: Candles, golden vessels [tapers, altar-cloths, images), and similar adornments are becoming, but they are not the adornment that properly belongs to the Church.

positions.statement: Images may be kept in churches as adornment or for teaching, but no honour is to be paid to them.
positions.mark: The passage allows images in churches for decoration or teaching while forbidding any honour or reverence toward them.
positions.excluded_by: The passage requires honour to images, or forbids images in churches altogether.
positions.first_defined: Apology of the Augsburg Confession (1531)

positions.name: Images not to be used in worship

defined.source: Heidelberg Catechism, Q&A 98 (1563)
defined.quote: But may not images be permitted in churches in place of books for the unlearned? A. No, we should not try to be wiser than God.

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 21.1 (1646)
defined.quote: under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture

positions.statement: Images have no place in churches or in worship; God is to be taught by the preached Word, not by pictures.
positions.mark: The passage says images must not be in churches or used in worship at all, not only that they must not be honoured.
positions.excluded_by: The passage approves images in churches, whether honoured or not.
positions.first_defined: Heidelberg Catechism (1563); Westminster Confession (1646)
positions.notes: Anglican Article XXII rejects worshipping images but does not forbid them; Anglicans are in neither 'permitted' nor 'rejected'.

shared_ground: God the Father, in his divine nature, cannot be pictured
Worship (latria) belongs to God alone
Idols of pagan gods are forbidden
The Incarnation made God visible in Christ (shared doctrine; not by itself an argument for icons)
queries: honour to the image passes to the original
notes: Hard: Epiphanius tearing a curtain image fits 'rejected'; Gregory the Great's 'books for the unlearned' fits 'permitted-not-venerated' unless he also approves honouring them.

tradition_notes.note: Not placed. Its canons and liturgy prescribe icons, but 'they have fallen out of use for many centuries, and have only remained in some Gospel lectionaries' (Diocese of California).

question: On what basis does God predestine people to salvation, and is anyone predestined to condemnation?

positions.name: Election to life only

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Epitome, XI.4 (1577)
defined.quote: The predestination or eternal election of God, however, extends only over the godly, beloved children of God, being a cause of their salvation

positions.statement: God's election by grace is the cause of the salvation of the elect; there is no corresponding decree of reprobation, and the lost perish by their own fault.
positions.mark: The passage says God's predestination is only to salvation and that those who perish are not passed over or ordained to it by God's decree.
positions.excluded_by: The passage says God decreed to pass by or condemn some; or that election rests on foreseen faith.
positions.first_defined: Formula of Concord, Article XI (1577)

positions.name: Election and reprobation (double predestination)

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 3.3 (1646)
defined.quote: By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life; and others foreordained to everlasting death.

defined.source: Canons of Dort, First Head, Article 15 (1619)
